questions.stem: In a nucleophilic substitution of a halogenoalkane, the nucleophile attacks

options.text: The carbon atom carrying the partial positive charge
options.explanation: The d+ carbon is the electron-seeking target of the electron-rich nucleophile.

options.text: The halogen atom carrying the partial negative charge
options.explanation: Nucleophiles seek positive centres, not negative halogens.

options.text: A hydrogen atom on the chain
options.explanation: Attack lands at the functional carbon, not random hydrogens.

options.text: The solvent molecules
options.explanation: Solvent is not the substrate.

questions.stem: Halogenoalkanes undergo nucleophilic substitution because

options.text: Carbon repels the nucleophile
options.explanation: It attracts it.

options.text: The C-X bond is polar, giving carbon a partial positive charge
options.explanation: The d+ carbon invites electron-pair donation.

options.text: The C-X bond is non-polar and unstable
options.explanation: The bond is polar, not non-polar.

options.text: The halogen donates electrons to carbon
options.explanation: The halogen withdraws electron density; it does not donate.

questions.stem: The species replaced by the nucleophile is

options.text: A hydrogen from the chain
options.explanation: No hydrogen leaves in substitution.

options.text: The solvent
options.explanation: Solvent is not part of the substrate.

options.text: The halogen atom bearing the partial negative charge
options.explanation: X departs with the bond's electron pair as X-.

options.text: An alkyl group of the chain
options.explanation: The skeleton stays intact.

questions.stem: Which option correctly describes the electronic role of the nucleophile?

options.text: It accepts an electron pair from carbon
options.explanation: That is electrophilic behaviour.

options.text: It removes a single electron, radical-style
options.explanation: No radical chemistry runs here.

options.text: It shares equally without net donation
options.explanation: Donation is directional and unequal.

options.text: It donates a lone pair of electrons into the d+ carbon
options.explanation: Pair donation forms the new C-Nu bond.

questions.stem: After the substitution, the halogen ends up as

options.text: A halide ion, X-, carrying the departed electron pair
options.explanation: Heterolytic departure hands both electrons to the halogen.

options.text: A neutral halogen molecule
options.explanation: No X2 forms in the substitution step.

options.text: A covalent acid HX
options.explanation: HX is not the immediate substitution product in alkali routes.

options.text: Still bonded to carbon
options.explanation: Substitution means it left.

questions.stem: Define nucleophilic substitution.
questions.modelAnswer: A reaction in which a nucleophile attacks a carbon with a partial positive charge and replaces the atom or group carrying the partial negative charge.

questions.stem: State why the C-X bond is polar.
questions.modelAnswer: The halogen is more electronegative than carbon, so it draws the bonding electrons and carries the partial negative charge.

questions.stem: Explain why the carbon of the C-X bond attracts nucleophiles.
questions.modelAnswer: The electronegativity difference leaves carbon electron-poor (d+), and electron-rich nucleophiles are attracted to exactly such centres.

questions.stem: Sketch reasoning: what happens to the electron pair of the C-X bond when the nucleophile attacks?
questions.modelAnswer: The pair departs entirely with the halogen as X-, so the carbon never exceeds four bonds - the incoming nucleophile's pair replaces the departing one.

questions.stem: In the OH- mechanism, the first curly arrow starts from

options.text: The solvent
options.explanation: No solvent arrow appears in the step.

options.text: The lone pair on the hydroxide oxygen
options.explanation: The donation begins at the electron source - the OH- lone pair.

options.text: The carbon atom of the halogenoalkane
options.explanation: Arrows show electron movement; carbon is the destination, not the source.

options.text: The halogen atom
options.explanation: The halogen's arrow runs in the opposite, departing direction.

questions.stem: The second curly arrow in the OH- mechanism shows

options.text: A hydrogen pair moving to oxygen
options.explanation: No hydrogen transfer occurs.

options.text: The C-C bond pair shifting
options.explanation: The skeleton stays intact.

options.text: The C-X bonding pair moving onto the halogen atom
options.explanation: The departing pair lands on X, making X-.

options.text: The O-H bond pair moving to hydrogen
options.explanation: No O-H arrow exists in this step.

questions.stem: The overall charge ledger for CH3CH2Br + OH- -> CH3CH2OH + Br- shows

options.text: Two negatives on the left and none on the right
options.explanation: Both sides carry exactly one negative charge.

options.text: Zero throughout
options.explanation: Ions are present on both sides.

options.text: A positive charge appearing mid-mechanism
options.explanation: No positive intermediate forms in the concerted step.

options.text: One negative charge on each side, carried by OH- then Br-
options.explanation: Neutral alcohol formation conserves the single negative unit.

questions.stem: Why does no intermediate form in the OH- substitution mechanism?

options.text: Attack and departure happen in one concerted step
options.explanation: The entering and exiting movements are simultaneous.

options.text: The carbon rejects any fifth bond
options.explanation: That is the consequence, not the step's classification.

options.text: The solvent blocks intermediates
options.explanation: Solvent does not forbid intermediates.

options.text: Bromide is too slow to leave
options.explanation: It leaves exactly as OH- arrives.

questions.stem: The product alcohol in the aqueous alkali mechanism forms because

options.text: Water adds across the chain
options.explanation: No addition chemistry runs in substitution.

options.text: The carbon-oxygen bond replaces the carbon-halogen bond
options.explanation: The OH group stays covalently attached to the carbon skeleton.

options.text: The hydroxide remains an ion in solution
options.explanation: It is consumed into the neutral alcohol.

options.text: The halogen donates electrons to oxygen
options.explanation: No such donation occurs.

questions.stem: Write the overall equation for bromoethane with aqueous OH-.
questions.modelAnswer: CH3CH2Br + OH- -> CH3CH2OH + Br-, the alcohol and bromide ion.

questions.stem: State the two curly arrows drawn in the OH- mechanism.
questions.modelAnswer: One from the OH- lone pair to the d+ carbon, one from the C-X bond onto the halogen as X- leaves.

questions.stem: Explain why the mechanism is described as substitution.
questions.modelAnswer: One group (OH) substitutes into the position vacated by another (Br), on an unchanged carbon skeleton - the defining pattern of substitution.

questions.stem: A student draws the OH- mechanism but forgets the negative charge on the departing bromide. Why is the drawing wrong?
questions.modelAnswer: The C-X bonding pair departs WITH the halogen, so bromide must carry the negative charge - omitting it breaks both the charge ledger and the electron bookkeeping.

questions.stem: The intermediate in the ammonia mechanism is

options.text: CH3NH2+ radical
options.explanation: No radicals form.

options.text: NH4OH
options.explanation: No such intermediate appears.

options.text: [CH3NH3]+Cl-, a substituted ammonium salt
options.explanation: Nitrogen carries four bonds and the positive charge after attack.

options.text: CH3NH2 free amine
options.explanation: That is the final product, after deprotonation.

questions.stem: The role of the second ammonia molecule is

options.text: To attack carbon a second time
options.explanation: The carbon already carries its nitrogen.

options.text: To replace the chloride ion
options.explanation: Chloride simply pairs with NH4+.

options.text: To catalyse the first step
options.explanation: Each ammonia is consumed stoichiometrically.

options.text: To remove a proton from the intermediate, forming NH4Cl and the free amine
options.explanation: Ammonia acts as base in the deprotonation beat.

questions.stem: In the first beat, where does the attacking lone pair of ammonia land?

options.text: The lone pair on ammonia's nitrogen to the d+ carbon
options.explanation: The nitrogen lone pair is the electron source.

options.text: The C-Cl bond to the carbon
options.explanation: The C-Cl pair departs to chlorine instead.

options.text: Chloride to nitrogen
options.explanation: Chloride is a spectator until pairing with NH4+.

options.text: A C-H bond to nitrogen
options.explanation: No C-H arrow exists here.

questions.stem: The co-product NH4Cl forms in step 2 because

options.text: The solvent supplies the proton
options.explanation: The proton comes from the intermediate's nitrogen.

options.text: The second ammonia keeps the removed proton, pairing with chloride
options.explanation: NH3 + H+ -> NH4+ alongside the existing Cl-.

options.text: Chloride attacks ammonia
options.explanation: Chloride has no attacking role.

options.text: Ammonia decomposes to nitrogen and hydrogen
options.explanation: No decomposition occurs.

questions.stem: Excess ammonia is used in this route to

options.text: Dissolve the halogenoalkane
options.explanation: Ethanol is the solvent.

options.text: Neutralise the ammonium chloride
options.explanation: No neutralisation is intended.

options.text: Prevent the amine product reacting further by substitution
options.explanation: Surplus NH3 out-competes the amine as nucleophile.

options.text: Speed up the deprotonation step only
options.explanation: The excess also guards against over-substitution.

questions.stem: Write the two equations for chloromethane with ammonia.
questions.modelAnswer: CH3Cl + NH3 -> [CH3NH3]+Cl-; then [CH3NH3]+Cl- + NH3 -> CH3NH2 + NH4Cl.

questions.stem: Name the final organic product and the inorganic co-product.
questions.modelAnswer: The primary amine (e.g. methylamine) and ammonium chloride.

questions.stem: Explain why the intermediate carries a positive charge on nitrogen.
questions.modelAnswer: After donating its lone pair, nitrogen holds four bonds (three H plus the carbon) and thus one unit of formal positive charge.

questions.stem: Sum the two ammonia steps into one overall equation for chloromethane.
questions.modelAnswer: CH3Cl + 2NH3 -> CH3NH2 + NH4Cl: one ammonia attacks, the second deprotonates, so two equivalents are consumed overall.
